Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Dependency request duration increases and caller deadlines expire. The caller can have normal CPU, memory, and database latency while the downstream service is slow.

## Distinguishing evidence

Follow the request trace into the named dependency, compare caller and callee duration, and check circuit-breaker state. If the callee has a specific database, DNS, or memory failure, attribute that root cause instead.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Inspect the named dependency and report the first failing hop with trace evidence.
2. Enable an existing safe fallback or circuit breaker and reduce retry amplification.
3. Use bounded retries only for idempotent operations; reconcile operations that may have completed after the deadline.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

The dependency completes within budget, timeout rate returns to baseline, and in-flight requests drain. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

Escalate to the downstream owner with the trace ID and failing time window. Do not increase every timeout without checking the end-to-end deadline. # gateway: Bad deploy and release regression

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Error rate rises shortly after a new version becomes active. Exceptions repeat on the new revision while healthy older replicas serve the same request.

## Distinguishing evidence

Compare deploy timestamp, image revision, and canary versus baseline errors. Look for configuration validation errors, missing fields, TypeError, or changed request contracts. A recent deploy alone does not establish causality.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Pause the rollout and compare errors by version before changing capacity.
2. If the new revision alone fails, roll back the image and its compatible configuration to the last known good release.
3. Check schema compatibility and feature flags before rollback; an irreversible migration requires the database owner.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

The prior revision serves the same request successfully and error rate returns to baseline for two observation windows. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the release owner if both revisions fail, no baseline exists, or rollback would cross an incompatible schema change. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Error rate rises shortly after a new version becomes active. Exceptions repeat on the new revision while healthy older replicas serve the same request.

## Distinguishing evidence

Compare deploy timestamp, image revision, and canary versus baseline errors. Look for configuration validation errors, missing fields, TypeError, or changed request contracts. A recent deploy alone does not establish causality.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Pause the rollout and compare errors by version before changing capacity.
2. If the new revision alone fails, roll back the image and its compatible configuration to the last known good release.
3. Check schema compatibility and feature flags before rollback; an irreversible migration requires the database owner.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

The prior revision serves the same request successfully and error rate returns to baseline for two observation windows. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the release owner if both revisions fail, no baseline exists, or rollback would cross an incompatible schema change. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# gateway: Dependency timeout and upstream request deadline

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Dependency request duration increases and caller deadlines expire. The caller can have normal CPU, memory, and database latency while the downstream service is slow.

## Distinguishing evidence

Follow the request trace into the named dependency, compare caller and callee duration, and check circuit-breaker state. If the callee has a specific database, DNS, or memory failure, attribute that root cause instead.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Inspect the named dependency and report the first failing hop with trace evidence.
2. Enable an existing safe fallback or circuit breaker and reduce retry amplification.
3. Use bounded retries only for idempotent operations; reconcile operations that may have completed after the deadline.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

The dependency completes within budget, timeout rate returns to baseline, and in-flight requests drain. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the downstream owner with the trace ID and failing time window. Do not increase every timeout without checking the end-to-end deadline. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# payments: Rate limit 429 and provider quota exhausted

Owner: payments on-call. Scope: payment authorization. Primary impact: card authorizations and order completion.

## Symptoms

Responses include HTTP 429 or resource quota exceeded. Repeated retries can amplify request volume even when CPU, memory, and database latency are normal.

## Distinguishing evidence

Read Retry-After, quota headers, request rate, retry rate, and the identity or tenant being limited. Distinguish dependency quota from local ingress admission limits.
Inspect authorization success, provider latency, ledger query time, and retry count. This service must authorize charges using a stable idempotency key; inspect payment provider and payment ledger as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Honor Retry-After and apply exponential backoff with jitter and a finite retry budget.
2. Reduce duplicate traffic and queue only work that can safely wait.
3. Coordinate a temporary quota increase with the provider after verifying the expected traffic source.

Service-specific constraint: Never blindly retry a charge. Reconcile the provider authorization ID and ledger entry first.

## Verify recovery

The limited identity remains below quota, 429 rate falls, and queued work drains without a new retry spike. Verify card authorizations and order completion with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the dependency owner for sustained expected traffic. Never bypass tenant isolation or rotate credentials to evade a quota. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

Owner: inventory on-call. Scope: stock availability and reservation. Primary impact: stock checks and reservation confirmation.

## Symptoms

Dependency request duration increases and caller deadlines expire. The caller can have normal CPU, memory, and database latency while the downstream service is slow.

## Distinguishing evidence

Follow the request trace into the named dependency, compare caller and callee duration, and check circuit-breaker state. If the callee has a specific database, DNS, or memory failure, attribute that root cause instead.
Inspect reservation failures, stock query duration, lock waits, and expired holds. This service must read available stock and write short-lived reservations; inspect stock database as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Inspect the named dependency and report the first failing hop with trace evidence.
2. Enable an existing safe fallback or circuit breaker and reduce retry amplification.
3. Use bounded retries only for idempotent operations; reconcile operations that may have completed after the deadline.

Service-specific constraint: Check reservation IDs and expiry before retrying writes; avoid overselling through duplicate reservations.

## Verify recovery

The dependency completes within budget, timeout rate returns to baseline, and in-flight requests drain. Verify stock checks and reservation confirmation with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the downstream owner with the trace ID and failing time window. Do not increase every timeout without checking the end-to-end deadline. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# gateway: Database query timeout and lock contention

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Database query duration and lock wait increase. Logs contain statement timeout, query deadline exceeded, or canceling statement. Application CPU may remain normal.

## Distinguishing evidence

Read database latency, lock waits, slow-query samples, and the configured statement deadline. Distinguish a slow query from an exhausted application connection pool by checking pool utilization and acquisition wait.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Identify the blocking query or slow query fingerprint and its transaction age.
2. Ask the database owner to cancel the confirmed blocker or apply the documented index/query mitigation.
3. Reduce nonessential query load; use bounded retries with jitter only for idempotent operations.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

Query p95 and lock wait return to baseline, the same operation completes, and timeout errors stop. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the database owner before terminating a transaction or changing a statement timeout. Increasing the timeout alone can increase congestion. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# gateway: Out of memory OOMKilled and heap exhaustion

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Resident memory approaches its container limit, processes restart, and logs or container events report OOMKilled, allocation failure, or exit code 137.

## Distinguishing evidence

Compare memory RSS with the configured memory limit and restart count. Verify exit reason; exit 137 without memory pressure can have other causes. Inspect heap growth, request size, and cache cardinality.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Shed oversized or nonessential requests and capture a bounded memory profile from a healthy replica.
2. Restore capacity with a known healthy replica or roll back a revision with confirmed increasing memory use.
3. Increase memory only after checking node headroom and setting an expiry for the temporary change.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

RSS stays below the limit with stable headroom, restart count stops growing, and representative requests succeed. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the service owner if memory grows monotonically or no safe replica has enough headroom; repeated restarts do not repair a leak. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# checkout: Out of memory OOMKilled and heap exhaustion

Owner: checkout on-call. Scope: order orchestration. Primary impact: order placement and cart conversion.

## Symptoms

Resident memory approaches its container limit, processes restart, and logs or container events report OOMKilled, allocation failure, or exit code 137.

## Distinguishing evidence

Compare memory RSS with the configured memory limit and restart count. Verify exit reason; exit 137 without memory pressure can have other causes. Inspect heap growth, request size, and cache cardinality.
Inspect order failures, dependency duration, pending reservations, and duplicate authorizations. This service must reserve stock and authorize payment before accepting an order; inspect payments and inventory as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Shed oversized or nonessential requests and capture a bounded memory profile from a healthy replica.
2. Restore capacity with a known healthy replica or roll back a revision with confirmed increasing memory use.
3. Increase memory only after checking node headroom and setting an expiry for the temporary change.

Service-specific constraint: An order can have a payment authorization even when the caller sees a timeout. Inspect its idempotency key before replay.

## Verify recovery

RSS stays below the limit with stable headroom, restart count stops growing, and representative requests succeed. Verify order placement and cart conversion with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the service owner if memory grows monotonically or no safe replica has enough headroom; repeated restarts do not repair a leak. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# gateway: CPU saturation and throttled workers

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

CPU utilization and throttled time are high, request duration increases, and worker queues grow without corresponding database or network latency.

## Distinguishing evidence

Compare CPU usage with quota, throttled periods, event-loop lag, queue depth, and request mix. Inspect a short CPU profile. Distinguish CPU-bound work from time waiting on a dependency.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Reduce optional expensive work and rate-limit the costly request class.
2. Scale workers only if downstream systems and node capacity have room.
3. Roll back a confirmed hot-loop regression or disable the responsible feature flag.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

CPU throttling and queue depth decline, throughput recovers, and request p95 returns to baseline. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the runtime owner when a profile shows a hot loop or scaling raises contention. Do not raise concurrency blindly. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# gateway: Connection pool exhausted and acquisition wait

Pool utilization reaches its maximum and requests wait for a connection. Logs report pool exhausted, acquire timeout, or too many clients while database execution can remain fast.

Measure pool active/max, pending acquisition count, acquisition wait, and database execution duration separately. Check leaked connections, long transactions, and total connections across replicas.

1. Find long-held or leaked connections and reduce admission of new database work.
2. Roll back a confirmed connection leak and ensure connections return to the pool in a finally block.
3. Adjust the pool limit only within the database connection budget; coordinate across all replicas.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

Pending acquisitions drain, active connections return below the limit, and requests complete without acquisition timeouts. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Connections fail before a TCP session begins. Logs contain NXDOMAIN, EAI_AGAIN, getaddrinfo failed, or a name resolution error.

Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Shed oversized or nonessential requests and capture a bounded memory profile from a healthy replica.
2. Restore capacity with a known healthy replica or roll back a revision with confirmed increasing memory use.
3. Increase memory only after checking node headroom and setting an expiry for the temporary change.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

RSS stays below the limit with stable headroom, restart count stops growing, and representative requests succeed. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the service owner if memory grows monotonically or no safe replica has enough headroom; repeated restarts do not repair a leak. Service-specific constraint: Never blindly retry a charge. Reconcile the provider authorization ID and ledger entry first.

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Dependency request duration increases and caller deadlines expire. The caller can have normal CPU, memory, and database latency while the downstream service is slow.

## Distinguishing evidence

Follow the request trace into the named dependency, compare caller and callee duration, and check circuit-breaker state. If the callee has a specific database, DNS, or memory failure, attribute that root cause instead.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Inspect the named dependency and report the first failing hop with trace evidence.
2. Enable an existing safe fallback or circuit breaker and reduce retry amplification.
3. Use bounded retries only for idempotent operations; reconcile operations that may have completed after the deadline.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

The dependency completes within budget, timeout rate returns to baseline, and in-flight requests drain. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the downstream owner with the trace ID and failing time window. Do not increase every timeout without checking the end-to-end deadline. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# gateway: Healthy service and stale alert verification

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Request error rate, latency, CPU, memory, storage, and dependency checks are within the service baseline. There are no corroborating recent failures.

## Distinguishing evidence

Check the alert evaluation timestamp, service labels, current time window, and successful representative requests. Missing telemetry is not evidence of health.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Verify that metrics and logs are fresh and correspond to the alerted service and environment.
2. Check a representative request and compare the alert window with the current window.
3. Record a recovered or stale alert only when fresh telemetry supports it; otherwise escalate as insufficient evidence.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

Fresh telemetry and successful requests consistently show normal operation across two windows. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

# gateway: Out of memory OOMKilled and heap exhaustion

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Resident memory approaches its container limit, processes restart, and logs or container events report OOMKilled, allocation failure, or exit code 137.

## Distinguishing evidence

Compare memory RSS with the configured memory limit and restart count. Verify exit reason; exit 137 without memory pressure can have other causes. Inspect heap growth, request size, and cache cardinality.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Shed oversized or nonessential requests and capture a bounded memory profile from a healthy replica.
2. Restore capacity with a known healthy replica or roll back a revision with confirmed increasing memory use.
3. Increase memory only after checking node headroom and setting an expiry for the temporary change.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

RSS stays below the limit with stable headroom, restart count stops growing, and representative requests succeed. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the service owner if memory grows monotonically or no safe replica has enough headroom; repeated restarts do not repair a leak. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# gateway: Bad deploy and release regression

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Error rate rises shortly after a new version becomes active. Exceptions repeat on the new revision while healthy older replicas serve the same request.

## Distinguishing evidence

Compare deploy timestamp, image revision, and canary versus baseline errors. Look for configuration validation errors, missing fields, TypeError, or changed request contracts. A recent deploy alone does not establish causality.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Pause the rollout and compare errors by version before changing capacity.
2. If the new revision alone fails, roll back the image and its compatible configuration to the last known good release.
3. Check schema compatibility and feature flags before rollback; an irreversible migration requires the database owner.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

## Verify recovery

The prior revision serves the same request successfully and error rate returns to baseline for two observation windows. Verify all storefront requests with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the release owner if both revisions fail, no baseline exists, or rollback would cross an incompatible schema change. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# checkout: Rate limit 429 and provider quota exhausted

Owner: checkout on-call. Scope: order orchestration. Primary impact: order placement and cart conversion.

## Symptoms

Responses include HTTP 429 or resource quota exceeded. Repeated retries can amplify request volume even when CPU, memory, and database latency are normal.

## Distinguishing evidence

Read Retry-After, quota headers, request rate, retry rate, and the identity or tenant being limited. Distinguish dependency quota from local ingress admission limits.
Inspect order failures, dependency duration, pending reservations, and duplicate authorizations. This service must reserve stock and authorize payment before accepting an order; inspect payments and inventory as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Honor Retry-After and apply exponential backoff with jitter and a finite retry budget.
2. Reduce duplicate traffic and queue only work that can safely wait.
3. Coordinate a temporary quota increase with the provider after verifying the expected traffic source.

Service-specific constraint: An order can have a payment authorization even when the caller sees a timeout. Inspect its idempotency key before replay.

## Verify recovery

The limited identity remains below quota, 429 rate falls, and queued work drains without a new retry spike. Verify order placement and cart conversion with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the dependency owner for sustained expected traffic. Never bypass tenant isolation or rotate credentials to evade a quota. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# payments: CPU saturation and throttled workers

Owner: payments on-call. Scope: payment authorization. Primary impact: card authorizations and order completion.

## Symptoms

CPU utilization and throttled time are high, request duration increases, and worker queues grow without corresponding database or network latency.

## Distinguishing evidence

Compare CPU usage with quota, throttled periods, event-loop lag, queue depth, and request mix. Inspect a short CPU profile. Distinguish CPU-bound work from time waiting on a dependency.
Inspect authorization success, provider latency, ledger query time, and retry count. This service must authorize charges using a stable idempotency key; inspect payment provider and payment ledger as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Reduce optional expensive work and rate-limit the costly request class.
2. Scale workers only if downstream systems and node capacity have room.
3. Roll back a confirmed hot-loop regression or disable the responsible feature flag.

Service-specific constraint: Never blindly retry a charge. Reconcile the provider authorization ID and ledger entry first.

## Verify recovery

CPU throttling and queue depth decline, throughput recovers, and request p95 returns to baseline. Verify card authorizations and order completion with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the runtime owner when a profile shows a hot loop or scaling raises contention. Do not raise concurrency blindly. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

# gateway: DNS resolution failure NXDOMAIN and resolver outage

Owner: gateway on-call. Scope: public HTTP ingress and request routing. Primary impact: all storefront requests.

## Symptoms

Connections fail before a TCP session begins. Logs contain NXDOMAIN, EAI_AGAIN, getaddrinfo failed, or a name resolution error.

## Distinguishing evidence

Resolve the exact dependency hostname from an affected container and a healthy container. Inspect DNS response codes, search domains, resolver latency, and recent service-name changes.
Inspect ingress error rate, route latency, upstream health, and active requests. This service must route /work requests to checkout while preserving trace IDs; inspect checkout as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Compare the configured hostname and service discovery record with the known good deployment.
2. Restore a missing service record or revert a verified hostname configuration change.

# inventory: Out of memory OOMKilled and heap exhaustion

## Symptoms

Resident memory approaches its container limit, processes restart, and logs or container events report OOMKilled, allocation failure, or exit code 137.

## Distinguishing evidence

Compare memory RSS with the configured memory limit and restart count. Verify exit reason; exit 137 without memory pressure can have other causes. Inspect heap growth, request size, and cache cardinality.
Inspect reservation failures, stock query duration, lock waits, and expired holds. This service must read available stock and write short-lived reservations; inspect stock database as part of the dependency boundary.

## Safe next steps

1. Shed oversized or nonessential requests and capture a bounded memory profile from a healthy replica.
2. Restore capacity with a known healthy replica or roll back a revision with confirmed increasing memory use.
3. Increase memory only after checking node headroom and setting an expiry for the temporary change.

Service-specific constraint: Check reservation IDs and expiry before retrying writes; avoid overselling through duplicate reservations.

## Verify recovery

RSS stays below the limit with stable headroom, restart count stops growing, and representative requests succeed. Verify stock checks and reservation confirmation with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.

## Rollback and escalation

Escalate to the service owner if memory grows monotonically or no safe replica has enough headroom; repeated restarts do not repair a leak. A mitigation needs an owner, a scope, a success check, and a rollback condition. Diagnostic evidence supports a recommendation; this runbook does not authorize autonomous production changes.

3. Increase memory only after checking node headroom and setting an expiry for the temporary change.

Service-specific constraint: Gateway replicas are stateless; route and timeout configuration changes affect every request.

# inventory: Bad deploy and release regression

Owner: inventory on-call. Scope: stock availability and reservation. Primary impact: stock checks and reservation confirmation.

## Symptoms

Error rate rises shortly after a new version becomes active. Exceptions repeat on the new revision while healthy older replicas serve the same request.

## Safe next steps

2. If the new revision alone fails, roll back the image and its compatible configuration to the last known good release.
3. Check schema compatibility and feature flags before rollback; an irreversible migration requires the database owner.

Service-specific constraint: Check reservation IDs and expiry before retrying writes; avoid overselling through duplicate reservations.

## Verify recovery

The prior revision serves the same request successfully and error rate returns to baseline for two observation windows. Verify stock checks and reservation confirmation with the service dashboard and one bounded representative request. Retain log IDs, metric timestamps, deploy revision, and trace IDs in the incident record.
